idiom_name: typed event-map hub (mitt<Events> or a typed EventEmitter wrapper)
implementation_notes: TypeScript does not change the runtime - Node's EventEmitter or the DOM's EventTarget still own the registry - but it moves the aggregator's contract into the type system: an event map interface or type declares every channel together with its payload, and a generic emitter (mitt<Events>, or EventEmitter subclassed with overloaded on/emit signatures) rejects unknown event names and mismatched payloads at compile time. The Subscriber role therefore collapses into a function type indexed by the event name, the Channel role becomes a key of the map, and publishing is emit() exactly as in JavaScript; the classic hand-written hub is still justified when events must be filtered, replayed or buffered asynchronously, which is where an RxJS Subject or a stream library earns its keep.
pitfalls: Only literal event names are checked: a name widened to string (from a constant, an enum member or JSON) silently compiles and emits an event nobody subscribes to.
Emit is synchronous and typed as void, so a handler that throws propagates into the publisher and an async handler's rejection is not awaited.
Types are erased at runtime, so mitt and EventEmitter cannot warn about a listener registered for an event that is never published - the map is a compile-time contract, not a runtime registry check.

Listener leaks are the same as in JavaScript: the typed overloads make off() convenient but nothing forces teardown, and handler identity must match exactly (a new arrow function unsubscribes nothing).
